concepts.explanation: Military control replacing normal civilian government and courts, usually during an emergency or coup.
A conflict where major powers back opposing sides instead of fighting each other directly.
Orders defining when and how troops may use force.
Unintended harm to civilians or property during a military operation.
A sudden, often violent, seizure of government power, usually by the military.
An armed rebellion against a government by irregular fighters, often using guerrilla tactics.
Cold War logic: neither side launches nuclear weapons because both would be destroyed in retaliation.
A border strip where military forces are banned by agreement, such as between North and South Korea.
Covert missions that a government will not acknowledge, often outside normal legal channels.
Accidentally attacking your own or allied forces.
A military court trying members of the armed forces for breaches of military law.
The harshest way to be expelled from the military, stripping benefits and carrying lasting stigma.
International treaties setting rules for treating prisoners, the wounded and civilians in war.
Airspace where aircraft are banned, enforced by threat of being shot down.
Destroying everything useful while retreating so the enemy cannot use it.
A spy or cell living normally in a target country, inactive until ordered to act.
Getting personnel out of a hostile area, often by helicopter or covert route.
Scouting enemy positions or terrain to gather information before acting.
One mission flown by one aircraft.
A military unit of roughly 300 to 1,000 soldiers, usually commanded by a lieutenant colonel.
An agreement to stop fighting. Not a peace treaty; the war is paused, not formally ended.
An official ban on trade with a country, used as pressure short of war.
Headquarters of the US Department of Defense. Often used to mean the US military leadership itself.
